Get the SDK and the example plugins
Tell Gradle where the SDK is (local.properties)
Signing: debug works out of the box

blocks.html:
Building a plugin is much lighter than building ATAK itself. This is the most common point of confusion, so let's clear it up first.

You are building a plugin, not ATAK core

The repository's BUILDING.md lists some heavy native prerequisites — NDK r12b, CMake 3.14.7, Conan, and modified copies of GDAL, ASSIMP, and tinygltf. Those are for compiling ATAK core from source. A plugin does not need any of them.

A plugin builds against the ATAK Plugin SDK, which ships the ATAK API as a prebuilt artifact. Your plugin's Gradle build pulls that API in; you never compile the C/C++ engine. So your toolchain is just a normal Android one plus the SDK.

What you actually need

Tool Notes
Android Studio The recommended IDE. A recent stable version is fine.
JDK 17 ATAK 5.x plugins compile against Java 17 (sourceCompatibility/targetCompatibility = VERSION_17).
Android SDK Installed via Android Studio's SDK Manager. The 5.x example targets compileSdk 36, targetSdkVersion 34, minSdkVersion 21. Build-tools are managed by the Android Gradle Plugin — no pinned buildToolsVersion.
The ATAK Plugin SDK pluginsdk.zip from the repo root, or the SDK matching your target ATAK version (the example targets ATAK_VERSION 5.6.0).
The **atak-gradle-takdev** plugin The Gradle plugin that teaches your build how to find and link the ATAK API. The 5.x example uses the 3.x line (takdevVersion = '3.+'), or a local atak-gradle-takdev.jar.
A signing key Debug signing works out of the box — atak-gradle-takdev generates a development keystore for you (see below).
A device/emulator with ATAK installed The matching CIV build, since the plugin loads into ATAK.

The ndk { abiFilters "armeabi-v7a", "arm64-v8a", "x86" } block you'll see in the plugin's build.gradle only filters which ABIs any bundled native libraries are packaged for. Unless your plugin ships its own .so files, you are not compiling native code and do not need the full NDK-r12b toolchain.

Get the SDK and the example plugins

From the open-source repository:

  • **pluginsdk.zip** — the Plugin SDK (API artifact + atak-gradle-takdev.jar).
  • **plugin-examples/helloworld** — a complete, working skeleton plugin. The best starting point and the source of every example in this guide.
  • **plugin-examples/plugintemplate** — a minimal template if you'd rather start from near-empty.

Unzip the SDK somewhere stable; you'll point Gradle at it next.

Tell Gradle where the SDK is (local.properties)

The plugin build reads everything environment-specific from local.properties at the project root. There are two ways it locates the ATAK API:

  • DevKit / repository mode — set takrepo.url (plus takrepo.user / takrepo.password) to point at an ATAK SDK Maven repository. When takrepo.url is present, the build uses the published atak-gradle-takdev plugin and pulls the API from that repo.
  • Local-jar mode — if takrepo.url is not set, the build falls back to a local atak-gradle-takdev.jar (by default expected near the project, at ../../atak-gradle-takdev.jar) and the local SDK.

Signing: debug works out of the box

In the ATAK 5.x example the debug build is already configured to sign with a development keystore that the atak-gradle-takdev plugin generates under the module's build directory — so you no longer have to set takDebug* keys in local.properties just to get a debug build running and installed. For release builds you supply and configure your own keystore (see Packaging & distribution).

That means a minimal local.properties only needs to point Gradle at the SDK:

# SDK location (repository mode)
takrepo.url=<your ATAK SDK maven repo URL>
takrepo.user=<user>
takrepo.password=<password>

Older ATAK 4.x plugins instead required takDebugKeyFile / takReleaseKeyFile (and their passwords/aliases) in local.properties, failing the build with No signing key configured! if absent. If you're porting a 4.x plugin you can drop that debug-key boilerplate.

gradle.properties in the example sets android.useAndroidX=true and android.enableR8=false — leave these as the SDK ships them unless you have a specific reason to change them.
